newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat Dalmatinska's 96 net shrinks to HRK14.8 mln.
newsitem.headline: Croat Dalmatinska's 96 net shrinks to HRK14.8 mln.

text.p: Dalmatinska Banka, one of Croatia's top 10 commercial banks, said on Wednesday net profit shrank to 14.8 million kuna in calendar 1996 from 15.3 million a year earlier despite generally stronger performance.
"The business itself was much better, but the government also took its share of our success through tax," finance director Mladen Fain told Reuters.
Dalmatinska is based in the coastal town of Zadar and has branches in the capital Zagreb and ports Split and Rijeka.

The bank's audited full-year results showed a rise in pre-tax earnings to 26 million kuna last year from 18.2 million in 1995. But tax more than tripled to 11.3 million kuna from less than three million on the 1995 results.
The bank plans to boost reserves by retaining more of last year's profits and paying slightly less in dividend, Fain said.
It will propose a dividend of 10 kuna per share -- equivalent to five percent of their nominal price -- to shareholders at an annual meeting on June 9, he added.
This is down from seven percent on face value of shares paid on the 1995 results. Dalmatinska split its stock last year, reissuing the outstanding shares at 200 kuna each.
"We could have paid an unchanged dividend, but decided to increase reserve funds instead," Fain said.
Dalmatinska's total 1996 income rose to 157.6 million kuna from 127.8 million on the back of higher interest income and commissions as it expanded operations and granted more loans.
But operating costs also consumed 26 million more last year, making a total of 96.2 million kuna.
"We think this is very good, although shareholders may not be as pleased and might argue we could have charged even higher interest," Fain said.

He said the bank's balance sheet had expanded around 16 percent to 1.66 billion kuna last year. This was mainly due to foreign credits, totalling 35 million German marks, although the deposit base also increased.
All available resources were channelled into new lending to private citizens and corporate clients.
Last year Dalmatinska advertised loans throughout the country and won clients from among companies outside its main area of Dalmatia on the Croatian seaboard, Fain said.
"Many avenues are open to us now...so our resources will be growing, but there are too few sound projects to invest in," he added, outlining this as a possible brake on credit growth.

The bank plans a new share issue later this year, but Fain declined to give further details before this is approved by shareholders. Dalmatinska has been mentioned among candidates likely to fully list their stock on Zagreb's bourse in 1997.
Its shares closed at 415 kuna on Tuesday, down five from last week. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
